references.text: Jacob mentions 'the Fear of my father Isaac' (פַּחַד יִצְחָק), the same expression used in v. 53 when he swears an oath. This is the closest parallel to Jacob's oath.
God identifies Himself as the God of Abraham and Isaac, which forms the background for Laban's invocation of the God of Abraham and Nahor as judge between them.
God reveals Himself to Isaac and confirms the promise given to Abraham, underscoring Isaac's relationship with God that Jacob refers to when he swears by 'the Fear of Isaac'.
Sarah says, 'The Lord will judge between me and you' – a parallel to Laban's invocation of God to judge between him and Jacob.
Abraham and Abimelech make a covenant with an oath, a parallel to the covenant-making and oath between Jacob and Laban.

Joshua reminds the people that Abraham's father Terah and Nahor served other gods, shedding light on Laban's reference to 'the God of Nahor' as possibly being a different deity than the God of Abraham.

Jacob uses the same covenant-titling formula ('the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac') as the legal basis for his oath against Laban and as the theological foundation for his prayer for mercy before meeting Esau.

Micah 7:20 theologically illuminates Genesis 31:53 by showing that Jacob's swearing by the God of the fathers is a concrete expression of the same covenant faithfulness that the prophet later celebrates as the basis for God's grace.
Both verses use the fixed covenant-titling formula ('the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob') to establish God's authority and continuity in relation to His people.
Acts 7:32 confirms that Jacob's swearing by 'the God of the fathers' is based on God's own self-presentation and identity as given in the Torah.
Acts 3:13 shows the continuity of God's identity from Jacob's time (Genesis 31) to the church, affirming that the same 'God of the fathers' is central in both the old and new covenants.
